Q1Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterWaves high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the fact that a pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics, so consecutive harmonics differ by 2f0 (260-220=40 Hz, giving f0=20 Hz), which is the organ-pipe content of Waves.
subtopic 1Organ Pipe
why this subtopicThe answer depends on a closed organ pipe having only odd harmonics, so consecutive harmonics differ by 2f0 and f0 = (260-220)/2 = 20 Hz.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are 220 Hz and 260 Hz. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?
  1. 30 Hz
  2. 40 Hz
  3. 10 Hz
  4. 20 Hz
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Two successive frequencies of closed pipe
  2. nv4l = 220 ...(i)
  3. (n + 2)v4l = 260 ...(ii)
  4. Dividing (ii) by (i), we get
  5. n + 2n = 260220 = 1311
  6. 11n + 22 = 13n
  7. n = 11
  8. So, 11v4l = 220
  9. v4l = 20
  10. So fundamental frequency is 20 Hz.

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. A tube closed at one end supports only odd harmonics: f = (2n-1) f0.
  2. Two nearest harmonics differ by 2f0: 2f0 = 260 Hz - 220 Hz = 40 Hz.
  3. f0 = 402 = 20 Hz.
  4. Check: 22020 = 11 and 26020 = 13 are consecutive odd integers, so f0 = 20 Hz, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRecall that a tube closed at one end supports only odd harmonics, f_n = n*f0 with n = 1, 3, 5, ... → Recognise that two nearest allowed harmonics therefore differ by 2*f0, and set the given difference (260 - 220) equal to 2*f0 → Solve for f0 by halving the difference, optionally checking that both given frequencies come out as odd multiples of it
whyThe work is one recall (closed pipe allows only odd harmonics) followed by one application: equating the gap between consecutive allowed harmonics to twice the fundamental and solving.
the catchOne option is exactly the frequency difference itself, which is what a candidate gets by applying the open-pipe rule (consecutive harmonics differ by f0) instead of the closed-pipe rule.

The trapoption 2Condition droppedcondition_misseddrop the condition the stem states and the option becomes true

The gap between the two printed frequencies, 260-220=40 Hz, is handed in as the fundamental, which is the rule for a pipe open at BOTH ends, so the stem's 'closed at one end' never enters the arithmetic.

Who fallsa student who carries the organ-pipe result as 'successive harmonics differ by the fundamental' without separating the open-open pipe from the closed-open one

Why it feels right40 Hz is the one number the stem hands over for free, and it divides into both 220 and 260

Also pullsoption 3

  2. badThe closed pipe is the quarter-wave case, so f0=40/4=10 Hz.The 4 belongs in f0=v/4L, not in the spacing; with f0=10 Hz these would be the 22nd and 26th harmonics, and a pipe closed at one end has no even harmonics.
No route to itoption 1

Q2Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterMechanical Properties of Fluids high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on equating hydrostatic pressure (P = h rho g) of the oil column and the water column at the same level in a U-tube manometer, which is fluid statics.
subtopic 1Problems on Hydrostatics
why this subtopicThe answer comes from equating hydrostatic pressure (P = h rho g) at the same level in both arms of the U-tube: 140 mm of oil balances 130 mm of water, so rho_oil = 1000 x 130/140 = 928 kg m^-3.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A U tube with both ends open to the atmosphere, is partially filled with water. Oil, which is immiscible with water, is poured into one side until it stands at a distance of 10 mm above the water level on the other side. Meanwhile the water rises by 65 mm from its original level (see diagram). The density of the oil is
  1. 800 kg m-3
  2. 928 kg m-3
  3. 650 kg m-3
  4. 425 kg m-3
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. hoil ρoil g = hwater ρwater g
  2. 140 × ρoil = 130 × ρwater
  3. ρoil = 1314 × 1000 kg/m3
  4. ρoil = 928 kg m-3

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Water rises 65 mm on the right, so it falls 65 mm on the oil side; the oil-water interface B is 130 mm below the final water level E.
  2. Oil top A is 10 mm above E, so hoil = 65 + 65 + 10 = 140 mm.
  3. Water column above level BC on the right: hw = 65 + 65 = 130 mm.
  4. Equal pressures at B and C: Pa + ρoil g hoil = Pa + ρw g hw.
  5. ρoil = ρw hwhoil = 1000 × 130140 ≈ 928.6 kg m-3.
  6. ≈ 928 kg m-3, which is option 2.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
22 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsUse conservation of water volume: the 65 mm rise on the water side means a 65 mm fall on the oil side, so the water column standing above the oil-water interface level (B-C) is 65 + 65 = 130 mm → Find the oil column height above the interface: 130 mm + 10 mm = 140 mm → Equate pressures at the common level B and C (both open to atmosphere): ρ_oil x g x 140 mm = ρ_water x g x 130 mm, and solve for ρ_oil
whyThe work is reading the interface geometry from the figure (doubling the 65 mm rise to get the 130 mm water head, adding 10 mm for the oil head) and then one hydrostatic pressure balance at the interface level.

Q3Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterOscillations high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the SHM relations v = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2) and a = omega^2*x, equated at x = 2 cm with A = 3 cm to give omega = sqrt(5)/2 and T = 2*pi/omega = 4*pi/sqrt(5), which is simple harmonic motion taught in Oscillations.
subtopic 1Calculate Time Period of SHM
why this subtopicThe answer is the time period T = 2*pi/omega, found by setting omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2) equal to omega^2*x at x = 2 cm, A = 3 cm, which gives omega = sqrt(5)/2 and T = 4*pi/sqrt(5).
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 3 cm. When the particle is at 2 cm from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is
  1. 4π5
  2. 2π3
  3. 5π
  4. 52π
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. v = ωA2 - x2
  2. a = xω2
  3. v = a
  4. ωA2 - x2 = xω2
  5. (3)2 - (2)2 = 2(2πT)
  6. 5 = 4πT
  7. T = 4π5

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. In SHM the speed at displacement x is |v| = ωA2 - x2.
  2. With A = 3 cm and x = 2 cm: |v| = ω9 - 4 = 5 ω.
  3. The acceleration magnitude is |a| = ω2 x = 2ω2.
  4. Setting |v| = |a|: 5 ω = 2ω2 ⇒ ω = 52 rad s-1.
  5. T = 2πω = 2π5/2 = 4π5 s, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsWrite the SHM speed at displacement x, v = ω*sqrt(A2 - x2), and the acceleration magnitude, a = ω2 * x, with A = 3 cm and x = 2 cm → Set the two magnitudes equal, ω*5 = 2*ω2, and solve for ω → Convert angular frequency to time period with T = 2*π/ω and match the option
whyThe work is recalling the two standard SHM expressions for velocity and acceleration at a displacement, equating them to solve for ω, then converting ω to the period.

Also pullsoption 4

  2. badCancel ω and the displacement together, leaving ω=5.Only one ω cancels; dividing by the 2 cm as well gives ω=52.

No route to itoption 2

Read through T=2πω this option means ω=3, i.e. A2-x2x2=3, which needs A=4 cm or x=1.5 cm. The stem prints 3 cm and 2 cm, and the quantities those two build - 9-4=5, 9+4=13, (3-2)2=1, 3×2=6 - contain no 3 and no 13, so no substitution reaches it.

Q4Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterGravitation high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the universal law of gravitation: with no external field, the two astronauts' mutual gravitational attraction pulls them towards each other.
subtopic 1Universal Law of Gravitation
why this subtopicThe answer depends on Newton's universal law of gravitation: any two masses attract each other, so with no other force acting the two astronauts move towards each other.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Two astronauts are floating in gravitational free space after having lost contact with their spaceship. The two will:
  1. Move away from each other
  2. Will become stationary
  3. Keep floating at the same distance between them
  4. Move towards each other
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Both the astronauts are in the condition of weightness.
  2. Gravitational force between them pulls towards each other.

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. In gravitational free space there is no external gravitational field, so →Fext = 0.
  2. The two astronauts still attract each other with F = G m1 m2r2, directed along the line joining them.
  3. This attraction is unopposed, so each accelerates towards the other while the centre of mass stays fixed; they move towards each other, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultyeasy · 1 step
stepsRecall that any two masses attract each other through mutual gravitation (Newton's law of universal gravitation), so with no external field the only force on each astronaut is the pull of the other, and they drift together
whyA single conceptual recall: in space free of external gravity, the astronauts' mutual gravitational attraction still acts, and nothing else does, so no calculation is needed.
the catchThe phrase 'gravitational free space' invites the misreading that no gravity acts at all, which points to the 'keep floating at the same distance' option.

why this chapterThe answer turns on the de Broglie relation lambda = h/sqrt(2mE) for a matter wave, with the thermal kinetic energy E = (3/2)kT substituted to give h/sqrt(3mkT), which is taught under de Broglie wavelength of matter waves in Modern Physics.
subtopic 1de Broglie Wavelength of Matter Waves
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the de Broglie relation lambda = h/p applied to a thermal neutron with kinetic energy (3/2)kT, giving lambda = h/sqrt(3mkT).
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with heavy water at a temperature T (Kelvin) and mass m, is
  1. 2h3mkT
  2. 2hmkT
  3. hmkT
  4. h3mkT
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. de-Broglie wavelength
  2. λ = hmv
  3. = h2m(KE)
  4. = h2m(32kT)
  5. λ = h3mkT

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. In thermal equilibrium at temperature T, the mean kinetic energy of the neutron is E = 32kT.
  2. Momentum from kinetic energy: p = 2mE.
  3. p = 2m · 32kT = 3mkT.
  4. λ = hp = h3mkT, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRecall that a thermal neutron in equilibrium at temperature T has mean kinetic energy E = 32kT → Convert kinetic energy to momentum: p = 2mE = 3mkT → Substitute into the de Broglie relation λ = h/p and match the resulting expression against the options

Q6Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterCapacitance high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on charge redistribution between capacitors in parallel and the energy stored in a capacitor (U = Q^2/2C, with the charge held fixed and the capacitance doubled), which the Capacitance chapter teaches.
subtopic 1Redistribution of Charges
why this subtopicThe answer depends on charge sharing between a charged and an identical uncharged capacitor (charge conserved, common potential halves), which makes the total energy Q^2/2(2C), half the original.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A capacitor is charged by a battery. The battery is removed and another identical uncharged capacitor is connected in parallel. The total electrostatic energy of resulting system
  1. Remains the same
  2. Increases by a factor of 2
  3. Increases by a factor of 4
  4. Decreases by a factor of 2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Charge on capacitor q = CV
  2. when it is connected with another uncharged capacitor.
  3. Vc = q1 + q2C1 + C2 = q + 0C + C
  4. Vc = V2
  5. Initial energy Ui = 12CV2
  6. Final energy Uf = 12C(V2)2 + 12C(V2)2
  7. = CV24
  8. Loss of energy = Ui - Uf
  9. = CV24
  10. i.e. decreases by a factor (2)

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Initial energy of the isolated charged capacitor: U = Q22C.
  2. With the battery removed, the total charge Q is conserved when the identical uncharged capacitor is connected.
  3. Two identical capacitors in parallel give C' = C + C = 2C.
  4. Final energy: U' = Q22C' = Q22(2C) = Q24C.
  5. U'U = Q2/4CQ2/2C = 12, so the energy decreases by a factor of 2, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsRecognise that with the battery removed the charge Q on the system is conserved (not the voltage) → Find the equivalent capacitance of the two identical capacitors in parallel (C becomes 2C) → Apply U = Q2/2C with the conserved charge and new capacitance and compare with the initial energy
whyThe work is identifying the conserved quantity (charge) after isolation, combining the capacitances in parallel, and substituting into the energy formula written in terms of Q to get the ratio.
the catchTrap option: using U = CV^2/2 while wrongly holding V fixed (as if the battery were still connected) gives exactly one of the listed options, so the choice of which quantity is conserved decides the answer.

Categories
TypeMCQmcqa question and four answers, nothing lettered or listed
AsksProportionalityrelationhow much one quantity changes when another does
ConceptOnce the battery is gone the charge is fixed, so sharing it with an equal capacitor doubles C at constant Q and halves U=Q22C
Why this answerThis question requires the quantity that stays fixed after disconnection to be identified before an energy formula is used, demonstrated by 'The battery is removed and another identical uncharged capacitor is connected in parallel'.
What catches a student
The trapoption 2Condition droppedcondition_misseddrop the condition the stem states and the option becomes true

The voltage is held at its old value, as though the battery were still across the plates, and U=12CV2 with C doubled then reads as twice the energy; the stem's 'The battery is removed' is exactly what forbids holding V fixed.

Who fallsa student who reaches for U=12CV2 and keeps V at the battery's emf out of habit

Why it feels rightthe capacitance plainly doubles, and with V fixed the energy formula is linear in C, so a factor of 2 looks forced on you

  1. okTwo identical capacitors in parallel give a total capacitance of 2C.
  2. badV is unchanged, so U=12(2C)V2 is twice the original energy.With the battery removed it is Q that is fixed, not V; the charge spreads over twice the capacitance so the shared voltage falls to V/2.
Also pullsoption 1

Who fallsa student who has just used conservation of charge to do the redistribution and carries the same bookkeeping over to the energy

Why it feels rightnothing leaves the pair of capacitors and the charge is conserved, so the stored energy looks like it must be conserved with it

  1. okThe charge Q is conserved when the uncharged capacitor is connected.
  2. badNothing escaped, so the stored energy stays the same.Charge is conserved here and energy is not: half of it is lost in the connecting wires as the charge flows, which is why Q22(2C) is half of Q22C.
No route to itoption 3

U=Q22C quadruples only if Q doubles while C is held fixed. The stem fixes the opposite: the added capacitor is 'identical', so C doubles, and 'uncharged', so Q does not change. Neither Q22C nor 12CV2 returns a factor of 4 under the stem's own substitution; the option sits beside option 2 as the other 'increases' entry.

  1. In all four drawings the diode arrow points from the left terminal toward R, so the anode (p-side) is on the left and the cathode (n-side) is on the right.

  3. Option 1: -2 V < +2 V, so the diode is reverse biased.
  4. Option 2: 3 V < 5 V, so the diode is reverse biased.
  5. Option 3: 0 V > -2 V, so the diode is forward biased.

Figure shows a circuit contains three identical resistors with resistance R = 9.0 Ω each, two identical inductors with inductance L = 2.0 mH each, and an ideal battery with emf ε = 18 V. The current 'i' through the battery just after the switch closed is

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · low
  1. Just after the switch closes, an inductor opposes any sudden change in current, so each inductor carries iL(0+) = 0 and behaves as an open circuit.
  2. Branch 1 (L in series with R): i1 = 0.
  3. Branch 2 (plain R): i2 = εR = 18 V9.0 Ω = 2 A.
  4. Branch 3 (R in series with L): with the inductor open and no capacitor considered (the stem lists only resistors, inductors and battery), i3 = 0.
  5. i = i1 + i2 + i3 = 0 + 2 + 0 = 2 A, which is option 1.
  6. Caveat: the figure draws an uncharged capacitor C across the second inductor; at t=0+ it would act as a short, giving i3 = 189 = 2 A and i = 4 A, which matches no option.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader

  3. dq = NRdφ

  5. Δ Q = ΔφtotalR
  6. = (NBA)R
  7. = μ0niπ r2R

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Field inside the long solenoid: B = μ0 n I, uniform over the coil since the coil radius 0.01 m is less than the solenoid radius 0.05 m.
  2. Flux linkage through the coil: NΦ = N μ0 n I π r2.
  3. Change in flux linkage as I goes from 4 A to 0: Δ(NΦ) = 100 × 4π × 10-7 × 2 × 104 × 4 × π (0.01)2.

  5. Charge through the coil: Q = Δ(NΦ)R = 3.2π2 × 10-410π2.

Q39Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterMagnetic Effect of Electric Current high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on resolving the Earth's horizontal field into two perpendicular vertical planes (cot^2 theta = cot^2 theta_1 + cot^2 theta_2), which is Earth's magnetism, listed under this chapter.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
If θ1 and θ2 be the apparent angles of dip observed in two vertical planes at right angles to each other, then the true angle of dip θ is given by
  1. cot2θ = cot2θ1 - cot2θ2
  2. tan2θ = tan2θ1 - tan2θ2
  3. cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2
  4. tan2θ = tan2θ1 + tan2θ2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. True dip satisfies tanθ = BVBH, so cotθ = BHBV.
  2. In a vertical plane at angle α to the magnetic meridian, the horizontal component is BHcosα while BV is unchanged, so tanθ1 = BVBHcosα, i.e. cotθ1 = cotθcosα.
  3. In the perpendicular vertical plane the horizontal component is BHsinα, so tanθ2 = BVBHsinα, i.e. cotθ2 = cotθsinα.
  4. Squaring and adding: cot2θ1 + cot2θ2 = cot2θ(cos2α + sin2α) = cot2θ.
  5. Hence cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2, which is option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

stepsFor a vertical plane at angle α to the magnetic meridian, keep the vertical component V unchanged and resolve the horizontal component to H cos(α), writing the apparent dip θ1 as the ratio of V to that effective horizontal component → Repeat for the perpendicular plane, where the effective horizontal component is H sin(α), giving the corresponding expression for θ2 → Combine the two expressions to eliminate the unknown α via sin2(α) + cos2(α) = 1, identify the surviving ratio with the true dip (tan θ = V/H), and match against the tan/cot, sum/difference option forms
whyThe work is resolving the horizontal field component into two perpendicular vertical planes, writing the apparent-dip ratio for each, and eliminating the unknown orientation angle with a trigonometric identity.
the catchApparent dip is not treated in NCERT and the Earth's magnetism section is absent from the current rationalised NCERT, so the resolution must be built without textbook support; the options form a tan/cot x sum/difference grid, so inverting the dip ratio (horizontal over vertical) leads straight to a matching wrong form.

  1. The leading strand away from replication fork
  2. The lagging strand away from the replication fork
  3. The leading strand towards replication fork

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Two DNA polymerase molecules work simultaneous at the DNA fork, one on the leading strand and the other on the lagging strand.
  2. Each Okazaki fragment is synthesized by DNA polymerase at lagging strand in 5' → 3' direction.
  3. New Okazaki fragments appear as the replication fork opens further.
  4. As the first Okazaki fragment appears away from the replication fork, the direction of elongation would be away from replication fork.

  1. DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 5' → 3' direction.
  2. On the template with polarity 3' → 5' the new strand (leading) grows continuously towards the replication fork, so Okazaki fragments are not used there.
  3. On the other template (5' → 3') the new strand (lagging) is made discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments, each synthesised 5' → 3', i.e. away from the replication fork, and later joined by DNA ligase.
  4. So Okazaki fragments elongate the lagging strand away from the replication fork, which is option 2.

Which of the following options gives the correct sequence of events during mitosis?
  1. Condensation → crossing over → nuclear membrane disassembly → segregation → telophase
  2. Condensation → arrangement at equator → centromere division → segregation → telophase
  3. Condensation → nuclear membrane disassembly → crossing over → segregation → telophase
  4. Condensation → nuclear membrane disassembly → arrangement at equator → centromere division → segregation → telophase
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. The correct sequence of events during mitosis would be as follows
  2. (i) Condensation of DNA so that chromosomes become visible occurs during early to mid-prophase.
  3. (ii) Nuclear membrane disassembly begins at late prophase or transition to metaphase.
  4. (iii) Arrangement of chromosomes at equator occurs during metaphase, called congression.
  5. (iv) Centromere division or splitting occurs during anaphase forming daughter chromosomes.
  6. (v) Segregation also occurs during anaphase as daughter chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.
  7. (vi) Telophase leads to formation of two daughter nuclei.

printed solution, as in the booklet

  1. Crossing over happens only in prophase I of meiosis, not in mitosis, so options 1 and 3 are wrong.
  2. In prophase chromatin condenses into chromosomes; by the end of prophase the nuclear envelope disassembles.
  3. In metaphase chromosomes align at the equator (metaphase plate).
  4. In anaphase centromeres split and sister chromatids segregate to opposite poles, followed by telophase.
  5. So the sequence is condensation → nuclear membrane disassembly → arrangement at equator → centromere division → segregation → telophase, which is option 4 (option 2 omits nuclear membrane disassembly).

            1. Option 1 is p-nitrophenol, option 2 is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid), option 3 is p-cresol (p-CH3C6H4OH) and option 4 is phenol.
            2. Electron-withdrawing -NO2 groups at ortho/para positions delocalise the negative charge of the phenoxide ion (-I and -R), stabilising it and increasing acidity.
            3. Electron-donating -CH3 destabilises the phenoxide ion, so p-cresol is less acidic than phenol.

            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · medium
            1. In m-bromoanisole the most acidic ring H is at C-2, flanked by the -I groups OCH3 and Br, so NH2- removes H at C-2.
            2. Loss of Br- from C-3 gives the benzyne with the triple bond between C-2 and C-3 (3-methoxybenzyne).
            3. NH2- adds to C-3 so that the resulting carbanion is at C-2, ortho to OCH3, where it is stabilised by the -I effect of oxygen.
            4. Protonation of the C-2 carbanion gives m-CH3OC6H4NH2 (m-anisidine) as A.
            5. NH2 occupies the same carbon that carried Br, so the net change is a substitution (not cine substitution); this matches option 3, while option 4 names the benzyne mechanism but shows the wrong product (o-anisidine).

            READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
            Which of the following pairs of compounds is isoelectronic and isostructural?
            1. IBr2-, XeF2
            2. IF3, XeF2
            3. BeCl2, XeF2
            4. Tel2, XeF2
            The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
            1. IBr2-, XeF2
            2. Total number of valence electrons are equal in both the species and both the species are linear also.

            → the working concludes: option 1

            printed solution, as in the booklet
            Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
            1. Count valence electrons in XeF2: 8 + 2(7) = 22.
            2. Xe in XeF2 has 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, so it is sp3d and the molecule is linear.
            3. Count valence electrons in IBr2-: 7 + 2(7) + 1 = 22, the same as XeF2.
            4. I in IBr2- has 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, so it is sp3d and linear, the same shape as XeF2.
            5. IF3 has 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, so it is T-shaped, not linear.
            6. BeCl2 has 2 + 2(7) = 16 valence electrons, so it is linear but not isoelectronic with XeF2.
            7. TeI2 has 6 + 2(7) = 20 valence electrons and 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs, so it is bent.
            8. Only IBr2- and XeF2 are both isoelectronic (valence shell) and isostructural, which is option 1.
